draft.title: Science and the ancient past
card: Scientists give historians evidence that written records and objects cannot. Their tests can be done on remains such as bones, wood, cloth and mummies.
Radiocarbon dating
finds the age of things that were once alive, such as bone, wood, seeds and linen. It cannot date stone or metal, because they were never alive.
DNA testing
reads the genetic code in remains. It can show who was related to whom, and some diseases a person had.
CT scans
use X-rays to make images of the inside of a mummy without unwrapping it. They can show broken bones, bad teeth, signs of illness and the objects wrapped inside.
draft.remember: Science can date once-living remains and reveal the lives of ancient people without destroying them.

a.q: Archaeologists find a wooden boat in an ancient harbour. Which method could find the age of the boat?
opts: Radiocarbon dating of the wood
A CT scan of the wooden planks
DNA testing of the harbour water
Radiocarbon dating of the harbour stones
a.why: Wood was once alive, so radiocarbon dating can find its age. A CT scan shows what is inside something and does not give its age. Stones were never alive, so they cannot be radiocarbon dated.
a.clue: Which method gives an age, and works on once-living things?

b.q: Researchers want to know if two Egyptian mummies were related, without unwrapping either one. Which method would give the best evidence of a family link?
opts: DNA testing of samples from each mummy
Radiocarbon dating of each mummy's linen
CT scans to compare the two mummies' teeth
Radiocarbon dating of the tomb's stone walls
b.why: DNA testing reads the genetic code, so it can show whether two people shared family. Radiocarbon dating gives an age, and two people of a similar age are not necessarily related. A CT scan can show body details, but it does not show family links.

b.best: DNA testing of samples from each mummy

proposal.title: Science and the ancient past
card: Scientists give historians evidence that written records and objects cannot. Some tests use up a small sample of remains, while others only take images.
Radiocarbon dating
finds the age of things that were once alive, such as bone, wood, seeds and linen. Stone and metal were never alive, so it cannot date them.
DNA testing
reads the genetic code in a small sample of bone or tissue. It can show who was related to whom, and some diseases a person had.
CT scans
use X-rays to make images of the inside of a mummy without unwrapping it. They can show broken bones, illness and worn teeth that hint at diet, but not family links.
proposal.remember: Radiocarbon dating gives an age, DNA shows family, and CT scans see inside the body.

opts: Radiocarbon dating of the wood

a.why: Wood was once alive, so radiocarbon dating can find its age. A CT scan shows what is inside something and does not give its age. Stones were never alive, so they cannot be radiocarbon dated.

b.q: Researchers want to know if two Egyptian mummies from one tomb were parent and child. Which method would give the best evidence?
opts: DNA testing of samples from each mummy
Radiocarbon dating of each mummy's linen
CT scans to compare the two mummies' teeth
Radiocarbon dating of the tomb's stone walls
b.why: DNA testing reads the genetic code in a small sample, so it can show who was related to whom. CT scans are tempting because they show the body in detail, but they cannot show family links. Radiocarbon dating only gives an age.

b.best: DNA testing of samples from each mummy
